Abstract.

We show that the generic fiber of a family f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S of smooth 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces always carries an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration, possibly after a finite extension of the base SS. In the particular case where the general fibers of the family are irrational surfaces, we establish that up to shrinking SS, such a family actually factors through an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X→Y\rho:X\rightarrow Y over a certain SS-scheme Y→SY\rightarrow S induced by the MRC-fibration of a relative smooth projective model of XX over SS. For affine threefolds XX equipped with a fibration f:X→Bf:X\rightarrow B by irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled surfaces over a smooth curve BB, the induced 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X→Y\rho:X\rightarrow Y can also be obtained from a relative Minimal Model Program applied to a smooth projective model of XX over BB.

2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
14R25; 14D06; 14M20; 14E30

Introduction

The general structure of smooth non complete surfaces XX with negative (logarithmic) Kodaira dimension is not fully understood yet. For say smooth quasi-projective surfaces over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, it was established by Keel and McKernan [10] that the negativity of the Kodaira dimension is equivalent to the fact that XX is generically covered by images of the affine line 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} in the sense that the set of points x∈Xx\in X with the property that there exists a non constant morphism f:𝔸1→Xf:\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow X such that x∈f⁡(𝔸1)x\in f(\mathbb{A}^{1}) is dense in XX with respect to the Zariski topology. This property, called 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruledness is equivalent to the existence of an open embedding X↪(X¯,B)X\hookrightarrow(\overline{X},B) into a complete variety X¯\overline{X} covered by proper rational curves meeting the boundary B=X¯∖XB=\overline{X}\setminus X in at most one point. In the case where XX is smooth and affine, an earlier deep result of Miyanishi-Sugie [14] asserts the stronger property that XX is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled: there exists a Zariski dense open subset U⊂XU\subset X of the form U≃Z×𝔸1U\simeq Z\times\mathbb{A}^{1} for a suitable smooth curve ZZ. Equivalently, XX admits a surjective flat morphism ρ:X→C\rho:X\rightarrow C to an open subset CC of a smooth projective model Z¯\overline{Z} of ZZ, whose generic fiber is isomorphic to the affine line over the function field of CC. Such a morphism ρ:X→C\rho:X\rightarrow C is called an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration, and we say that ρ\rho is of affine type or complete type when the base curve CC is affine or complete, respectively.

Smooth 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled but not 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine varieties are known to exist in every dimension ≥3\geq 3 [1]. Many examples of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-uniruled affine threefolds can be constructed in the form of flat families f:X→Bf:X\rightarrow B of smooth 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces parametrized by a smooth base curve BB. For instance, the complement XX of a smooth cubic surface S⊂ℙℂ3S\subset\mathbb{P}_{\mathbb{C}}^{3} is the total space of a family f:X→𝔸1=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[t])f:X\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[t]) of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled surfaces induced by the restriction of a pencil f¯:ℙ3⇢ℙ1\overline{f}:\mathbb{P}^{3}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} on ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} generated by SS and three times a tangent hyperplane HH to SS whose intersection with SS consists of a cuspidal cubic curve. The general fibers of ff have negative Kodaira dimension, carrying 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations of complete type only, and the failure of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness is intimately related to the fact that the generic fiber XηX_{\eta} of ff, which is a surface defined over the field K=ℂ⁡(t)K=\mathbb{C}(t), does not admit any 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration defined over ℂ⁡(t)\mathbb{C}(t). Nevertheless, it was noticed in [3, Theorem 6.1] that one can infer straight from the construction of f:X→𝔸1f:X\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1} the existence a finite base extension Spec⁡(L)→Spec⁡(K)\mathrm{Spec}(L)\rightarrow\mathrm{Spec}(K) for which the surface Xη×Spec⁡(K)Spec⁡(L)X_{\eta}\times_{\mathrm{Spec}(K)}\mathrm{Spec}(L) carries an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:Xη×Spec⁡(K)Spec⁡(L)→ℙL1\rho:X_{\eta}\times_{\mathrm{Spec}(K)}\mathrm{Spec}(L)\rightarrow\mathbb{P}_{L}^{1} defined over the field LL.

A natural question is then to decide whether this phenomenon holds in general for families f:X→Bf:X\rightarrow B of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces parameterized by a smooth base curve BB, namely, does the existence of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations on the general fibers of ff imply the existence of one on the generic fiber of ff, possibly after a finite extension of the base BB ? A partial positive answer is given by Gurjar-Masuda-Miyanishi in [3, Theorem 3.8] under the additional assumption that the general fibers of ff carry 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations of affine type. The main result in loc. cit. is derived from the study of log-deformations of suitable relative normal projective models f¯:(X¯,D)→B\overline{f}:(\overline{X},D)\rightarrow B of XX over BB with appropriate boundaries DD. It is established in particular that the structure of the boundary divisor of a well chosen smooth projective completion of a general closed fiber XsX_{s} is stable under small deformations, a property which implies in turn, possibly after a finite extension of the base BB, the existence of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration of affine type on the generic fiber of ff. This log-deformation theoretic approach is also central in the related recent work of Flenner-Kaliman-Zaidenberg [2] on the classification of normal affine surfaces with 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations of affine type up to a certain notion of deformation equivalence, defined for families which admit suitable relative projective models satisfying Kamawata’s axioms of logarithmic deformations of pairs [8]. The fact that the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations under consideration are of affine type plays again a crucial role and, in contrast with the situation considered in [3], the restrictions imposed on the families imply the existence of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations of affine type on their generic fibers.

Our main result (Theorem 6) consists of a generalization of the results in [3] to families f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled surfaces over an arbitrary normal base SS, which also includes the case where a general closed fiber XsX_{s} of ff admits 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations of complete type only. In particular, we obtain the following positive answer to Conjecture 6.2 in [3]:

Theorem.

Let f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S be dominant morphism between normal complex algebraic varieties whose general fibers are smooth 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces. Then there exists a dense open subset S∗⊂SS_{*}\subset S, a finite étale morphism T→S∗T\rightarrow S_{*} and a normal TT-scheme h:Y→Th:Y\rightarrow T such that the induced morphism fT=p​rT:XT=X×S∗T→Tf_{T}=\mathrm{p}r_{T}:X_{T}=X\times_{S_{*}}T\rightarrow T factors as

fT=h∘ρ:XT⟶ρY⟶hT,f_{T}=h\circ\rho:X_{T}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rho}}{{\longrightarrow}}Y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle h}}{{\longrightarrow}}T,

where ρ:XT→Y\rho:X_{T}\rightarrow Y is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration.

In contrast with the log-deformation theoretic strategy used in [3], which involves the study of certain Hilbert schemes of rational curves on well-chosen relative normal projective models f¯:(X¯,B)→S\overline{f}:(\overline{X},B)\rightarrow S of XX over SS, our approach is more elementary, based on the notion of Kodaira dimension [7] adapted to the case of geometrically connected varieties defined over arbitrary base fields of characteristic zero. Indeed, the hypothesis means equivalently that the general fibers of ff have negative Kodaira dimension. This property is in turn inherited by the generic fiber of ff, which is a smooth affine surface defined over the function field of SS, thanks to a standard Lefschetz principle argument. Then we are left with checking that a smooth affine surface XX defined over an arbitrary base field kk of characteristic zero and with negative Kodaira dimension admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration, possibly after a suitable finite base extension Spec⁡(k0)→Spec⁡(k)\mathrm{Spec}(k_{0})\rightarrow\mathrm{Spec}(k), a fact which follows immediately from finite type hypotheses and the aforementioned characterization of Miyanishi-Sugie [14].

The article is organized as follows. The first section contains a review of the structure of smooth affine surfaces of negative Kodaira dimension over arbitrary base fields kk of characteristic zero. We show in particular that every such surface XX admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration after a finite extension of the base field kk, and we give criteria for the existence of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations defined over kk. These results are then applied in the second section to the study of deformations f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S of smooth 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces: after giving the proof of the main result, Theorem 6, we consider in more detail the particular situation where the general fibers of f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S are irrational. In this case, after shrinking SS if necessary, we show that the morphism ff actually factors through an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X→Y\rho:X\rightarrow Y over an SS-scheme h:Y→Sh:Y\rightarrow S which coincides, up to birational equivalence, with the Maximally Rationally Connected quotient of a relative smooth projective model f¯:X¯→S\overline{f}:\overline{X}\rightarrow S of XX over SS. The last section is devoted to the case of affine threefolds equipped with a fibration f:X→Bf:X\rightarrow B by irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled surfaces over a smooth base curve BB: we explain in particular how to construct an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X→Y\rho:X\rightarrow Y factoring ff by means of a relative Minimal Model Program applied to a smooth projective model f¯:X¯→B\overline{f}:\overline{X}\rightarrow B of XX over BB.

1. 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruledness of affine surfaces over non closed field

1.1. Logarithmic Kodaira dimension

1.1.1.

Let XX be a smooth geometrically connected algebraic variety defined over a field kk of characteristic zero. By virtue of Nagata compactification [15] and Hironaka desingularization [5] theorems, there exists an open immersion X↪(X¯,B)X\hookrightarrow(\overline{X},B) into a smooth complete algebraic variety X¯\overline{X} with reduced SNC boundary divisor B=X¯∖XB=\overline{X}\setminus X. The (logarithmic) Kodaira dimension κ⁡(X)\kappa(X) of XX is then defined as the Iitaka dimension [6] of the pair (X¯;ωX¯​(log⁡B))(\overline{X};\omega_{\overline{X}}(\log B)) where ωX¯​(log⁡B)=(detΩX¯/k1)⊗𝒪X¯​(B)\omega_{\overline{X}}(\log B)=(\det\Omega_{\overline{X}/k}^{1})\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\overline{X}}(B). So letting ℛ⁡(X¯,B)=⨁m≥0H0​(X¯,ωX¯​(log⁡B)⊗m)\mathcal{R}(\overline{X},B)=\bigoplus_{m\geq 0}H^{0}(\overline{X},\omega_{\overline{X}}(\log B)^{\otimes m}), we have κ⁡(X)=tr.degk⁡ℛ⁡(X¯,B)−1\kappa(X)=\mathrm{tr}.\deg_{k}\mathcal{R}(\overline{X},B)-1 if H0​(X¯,ωX¯​(log⁡B)⊗m)≠0H^{0}(\overline{X},\omega_{\overline{X}}(\log B)^{\otimes m})\neq 0 for sufficiently large mm. Otherwise, if H0​(X¯,ωX¯​(log⁡B)⊗m)=0H^{0}(\overline{X},\omega_{\overline{X}}(\log B)^{\otimes m})=0 for every m≥1m\geq 1, we set by convention κ⁡(X)=−∞\kappa(X)=-\infty and we say that κ⁡(X)\kappa(X) is negative. The so-defined element κ⁡(X)∈{0,…,dimk​X}∪{−∞}\kappa(X)\in\left\{0,\ldots,\mathrm{dim}_{k}X\right\}\cup\{-\infty\} is independent of the choice of a smooth complete model (X¯,B)(\overline{X},B) [7].

Furthermore, the Kodaira dimension of XX is invariant under arbitrary extensions of the base field kk. Indeed, given an extension k⊂k′k\subset k^{\prime}, the pair (X¯k′,Bk′)(\overline{X}_{k^{\prime}},B_{k^{\prime}}) obtained by the base change Spec⁡(k′)→Spec⁡(k)\mathrm{Spec}(k^{\prime})\rightarrow\mathrm{Spec}(k) is a smooth complete model of Xk′=X×Spec⁡(k)Spec⁡(k′)X_{k^{\prime}}=X\times_{\mathrm{Spec}(k)}\mathrm{Spec}(k^{\prime}) with reduced SNC boundary Bk′B_{k^{\prime}}. Furthermore letting π:X¯k′→X¯\pi:\overline{X}_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow\overline{X} be the corresponding faithfully flat morphism, we have ωX¯k′​(log⁡Bk′)≃π∗​ωX​(log⁡B)\omega_{\overline{X}_{k^{\prime}}}(\log B_{k^{\prime}})\simeq\pi^{*}\omega_{X}(\log B) and so ℛ⁡(Xk′)≃ℛ⁡(X)⊗kk′\mathcal{R}(X_{k^{\prime}})\simeq\mathcal{R}(X)\otimes_{k}k^{\prime} by the flat base change theorem [4, Proposition III.9.3]. Thus κ⁡(X)=κ⁡(Xk′)\kappa(X)=\kappa(X_{k^{\prime}}).

Example 1.

The affine line 𝔸k1\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1} is the only smooth geometrically connected non complete curve CC with negative Kodaira dimension. Indeed, let C¯\overline{C} be a smooth projective model of CC and let C¯k¯\overline{C}_{\overline{k}} be the curve obtained by the base change to an algebraic closure k¯\overline{k} of kk. Since CC is non complete, B=C¯k¯∖Ck¯B=\overline{C}_{\overline{k}}\setminus C_{\overline{k}} consists of a finite collection of closed points p1,…​psp_{1},\ldots p_{s}, s≥1s\geq 1, on which the Galois group Gal⁡(k¯/k)\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{k}/k) acts by kk-automorphisms of C¯k¯\overline{C}_{\overline{k}}. Clearly, H0​(C¯k¯,ωC¯k¯​(log⁡B)⊗m)≠0H^{0}(\overline{C}_{\overline{k}},\omega_{\bar{C}_{\overline{k}}}(\log B)^{\otimes m})\neq 0 unless C¯k¯≃ℙk¯1\overline{C}_{\overline{k}}\simeq\mathbb{P}_{\overline{k}}^{1} and s=1s=1. Since p1p_{1} is then necessarily Gal⁡(k¯/k)\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{k}/k)-invariant, C¯∖C\overline{C}\setminus C consists of unique kk-rational point, showing that C¯≃ℙk1\overline{C}\simeq\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1} and C≃𝔸k1C\simeq\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1}.

1.2. Smooth affine surfaces with negative Kodaira dimension


Recall that by virtue of [14], a smooth affine surface XX defined over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero has negative Kodaira dimension if and only if it is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled: there exists a Zariski dense open subset U⊂XU\subset X of the form U≃Z×𝔸1U\simeq Z\times\mathbb{A}^{1} for a suitable smooth curve ZZ. In fact, the projection prZ:U≃Z×𝔸1→Z\mathrm{pr}_{Z}:U\simeq Z\times\mathbb{A}^{1}\rightarrow Z always extends to an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X→C\rho:X\rightarrow C over an open subset CC of a smooth projective model Z¯\overline{Z} of ZZ. This characterization admits the following straightforward generalization to arbitrary base fields of characteristic zero:

Theorem 2.

Let XX be a smooth geometrically connected affine surface defined over a field kk of characteristic zero. Then the following are equivalent:

a) The Kodaira dimension κ⁡(X)\kappa(X) of XX is negative.

b) For some finite extension k0k_{0} of kk, the surface Xk0X_{k_{0}} contains an open subset U≃Z×𝔸k01U\simeq Z\times\mathbb{A}_{k_{0}}^{1} for some smooth curve ZZ defined over k0k_{0}.

c) There exists a finite extension k0k_{0} of kk and an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:Xk0→C0\rho:X_{k_{0}}\rightarrow C_{0} over a smooth curve C0C_{0} defined over k0k_{0}.

Proof.

Clearly c) implies b) and b) implies a). To show that a) implies c), we observe that letting k¯\overline{k} be an algebraic closure of kk, we have κ⁡(Xk¯)=κ⁡(X)<0\kappa(X_{\overline{k}})=\kappa(X)<0. It then follows from the aforementioned result of Miyanishi-Sugie [14] that Xk¯X_{\overline{k}} admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration q:Xk¯→Cq:X_{\overline{k}}\rightarrow C over a smooth curve CC, with smooth projective model C¯\overline{C}. Since Xk¯X_{\overline{k}} and C¯\overline{C} are of finite type over k¯\overline{k}, there exists a finite extension k⊂k0k\subset k_{0} such that q:Xk¯→C¯q:X_{\overline{k}}\rightarrow\overline{C} is obtained from a morphism ρ:Xk0→C¯0\rho:X_{k_{0}}\rightarrow\overline{C}_{0} to a smooth projective curve C¯0\overline{C}_{0} defined over k0k_{0} by the base extension Spec⁡(k¯)→Spec⁡(k0)\mathrm{\mathrm{Spec}}(\overline{k})\rightarrow\mathrm{Spec}(k_{0}). By virtue of Example 1, ρ:Xk0→C¯0\rho:X_{k_{0}}\rightarrow\overline{C}_{0} is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration. ∎

Examples of smooth affine surfaces XX of negative Kodaira dimension without any 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration defined over the base field but admitting 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations of complete type after a finite base extension were already constructed in [1]. The following example illustrates the fact that a similar phenomenon occurs for 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations of affine type, providing in particular a negative answer to Problem 3.13 in [3].

Example 3.

Let B⊂ℙk2=Proj⁡(k⁡[x,y,z])B\subset\mathbb{P}_{k}^{2}=\mathrm{Proj}(k[x,y,z]) be a smooth conic without kk-rational points defined by a quadratic form q=x2+a​y2+b​z2q=x^{2}+ay^{2}+bz^{2}, where a,b∈k∗a,b\in k^{*}, and let X¯⊂ℙk3=Proj⁡(k⁡[x,y,z,t])\overline{X}\subset\mathbb{P}_{k}^{3}=\mathrm{Proj}(k[x,y,z,t]) be the smooth quadric surface defined by the equation q⁡(x,y,z)−t2=0q(x,y,z)-t^{2}=0. The complement X⊂X¯X\subset\overline{X} of the hyperplane section {t=0}\left\{t=0\right\} is a kk-rational smooth affine surface with κ⁡(X)<0\kappa(X)<0, which does not admit any 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X→C\rho:X\rightarrow C over a smooth, affine or projective curve CC. Indeed, if such a fibration existed then a smooth projective model of CC would be isomorphic to ℙk1\mathbb{P}_{k}^{1}; since the fiber of ρ\rho over a general kk-rational point of CC is isomorphic to 𝔸k1\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1}, its closure in X¯\overline{X} would intersect the boundary X¯∖X≃B\overline{X}\setminus X\simeq B in a unique point, necessarily kk-rational, in contradiction with the choice of BB.

In constrast, for a suitable finite extension k⊂k′k\subset k^{\prime}, the surface Xk′X_{k^{\prime}} becomes isomorphic to the complement of the diagonal in X¯k′≃ℙk′1×ℙk′1\overline{X}_{k^{\prime}}\simeq\mathbb{P}_{k^{\prime}}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}_{k^{\prime}}^{1} and hence, it admits at least two distinct 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations over ℙk′1\mathbb{P}_{k^{\prime}}^{1}, induced by the restriction of the first and second projections from X¯k′\overline{X}_{k^{\prime}}. Furthermore, since Xk′X_{k^{\prime}} is isomorphic to the smooth affine quadric in 𝔸k′3=Spec⁡(k′​[u,v,w])\mathbb{A}_{k^{\prime}}^{3}=\mathrm{Spec}(k^{\prime}[u,v,w]) with equation u​v−w2=1uv-w^{2}=1, it also admits two distinct 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations over 𝔸k′1\mathbb{A}_{k^{\prime}}^{1}, induced by the restrictions of the projections pru\mathrm{pr}_{u} and prv\mathrm{pr}_{v}.

1.3. Existence of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations defined over the base field

1.3.1.

The previous example illustrates the general fact that if XX is a smooth geometrically connected affine surface with κ⁡(X)<0\kappa(X)<0 which does not admit any 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration, then there exists a finite extension k′k^{\prime} of kk such that Xk′X_{k^{\prime}} admits at least two 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations of the same type, either affine or complete, with distinct general fibers. Indeed, by virtue of Theorem 2, there exists a finite extension k0k_{0} of kk such that Xk0X_{k_{0}} admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:Xk0→C\rho:X_{k_{0}}\rightarrow C. Let k′k^{\prime} be the Galois closure of k0k_{0} in an algebraic closure of kk and let ρk′:Xk′→Ck′\rho_{k^{\prime}}:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C_{k^{\prime}} be the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration deduced from ρ\rho. If ρk′:Xk′→Ck′\rho_{k^{\prime}}:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C_{k^{\prime}} is globally invariant under the action of the Galois group Gal⁡(k′/k)\mathrm{Gal}(k^{\prime}/k) on Xk′X_{k^{\prime}}, in the sense that for every Φ∈Gal⁡(k′/k)\Phi\in\mathrm{Gal}(k^{\prime}/k) considered as a Galois automorphism of Xk′X_{k^{\prime}} there exists a commutative diagram

Xk′\displaystyle X_{k^{\prime}} →Φ\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\Phi}}{{\rightarrow}} Xk′\displaystyle X_{k^{\prime}}
ρk′↓\displaystyle\rho_{k^{\prime}}\downarrow ↓ρk′\displaystyle\downarrow\rho_{k^{\prime}}
Ck′\displaystyle C_{k^{\prime}} →φ\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\varphi}}{{\rightarrow}} Ck′\displaystyle C_{k^{\prime}}

for a certain k′k^{\prime}-automorphism φ\varphi of Ck′C_{k^{\prime}}, then we would obtain a Galois action of Gal⁡(k′/k)\mathrm{Gal}(k^{\prime}/k) on Ck′C_{k^{\prime}} for which ρk′:Xk′→Ck′\rho_{k^{\prime}}:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C_{k^{\prime}} becomes an equivariant morphism. Since Ck′C_{k^{\prime}} is quasi-projective and ρk′\rho_{k}^{\prime} is affine, it would follow from Galois descent that there exists a curve C~\tilde{C} defined over kk and a morphism q:X→C~q:X\rightarrow\tilde{C} defined over kk such that ρk′:Xk′→Ck′\rho_{k^{\prime}}:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C_{k^{\prime}} is obtained from qq by the base change Spec⁡(k′)→Spec⁡(k)\mathrm{Spec}(k^{\prime})\rightarrow\mathrm{Spec}(k). Since by virtue of Example 1 the affine line does not have any nontrivial form, the generic fiber of qq would be isomorphic to the affine line over the field of rational functions of C~\tilde{C} and so, q:X→C~q:X\rightarrow\tilde{C} would be an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration defined over kk, in contradiction with our hypothesis. So there exists at least an element Φ∈Gal⁡(k′/k)\Phi\in\mathrm{Gal}(k^{\prime}/k) considered as a kk-automorphism of Xk′X_{k^{\prime}} such that the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations ρk′:Xk′→Ck′\rho_{k^{\prime}}:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C_{k^{\prime}} and ρk′∘φ:Xk′→Ck′\rho_{k^{\prime}}\circ\varphi:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C_{k^{\prime}} have distinct general fibers.

Arguing backward, we obtain the following useful criterion:

Proposition 4.

Let XX be a smooth geometrically connected affine surface with κ⁡(X)<0\kappa(X)<0. If there exists a finite Galois extension k′k^{\prime} of kk such that Xk′X_{k^{\prime}} admits a unique 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ′:Xk′→Ck′\rho^{\prime}:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C_{k^{\prime}} up to composition by automorphisms of Ck′C_{k^{\prime}}, then ρ′:Xk′→Ck′\rho^{\prime}:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C_{k^{\prime}} is obtained by base extension from an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X→C\rho:X\rightarrow C defined over kk.

Corollary 5.

A smooth geometrically connected irrational affine surface XX has negative Kodaira dimension if and only if it admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X→C\rho:X\rightarrow C over a smooth irrational curve CC defined over the base field kk. Furthermore for every extension k′k^{\prime} of kk, ρk′:Xk′→Ck′\rho_{k^{\prime}}:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C_{k^{\prime}} is the unique 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration on Xk′X_{k^{\prime}} up to composition by automorphisms of Ck′C_{k^{\prime}}.

Proof.

Uniqueness is clear since otherwise Ck′C_{k^{\prime}} would be dominated by a general fiber of another 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration on Xk′X_{k^{\prime}}, and hence would be rational, implying in turn the rationality of XX. By virtue of Theorem 2, there exists a finite Galois extension k′k^{\prime} of kk and an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ′:Xk′→C′\rho^{\prime}:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C^{\prime} over a smooth curve C′C^{\prime}. The latter is irrational as XX is irrational, which implies that ρ′:Xk′→C′\rho^{\prime}:X_{k^{\prime}}\rightarrow C^{\prime} is the unique 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration on Xk′X_{k^{\prime}}. So ρ′\rho^{\prime} descend to an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X→C\rho:X\rightarrow C over a smooth irrational curve CC defined over kk. ∎

2. Families of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces

2.1. Existence of étale 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylinders

This subsection is devoted to the proof of the following:

Theorem 6.

Let XX and SS be normal algebraic varieties defined over a field kk of infinite transcendence degree over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, and let f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S be a dominant affine morphism with the property that for a general closed point s∈Ss\in S, the fiber XsX_{s} is a smooth geometrically connected affine surface with negative Kodaira dimension. Then there exists an open subset S∗⊂SS_{*}\subset S, a finite étale morphism T→S∗T\rightarrow S_{*} and a normal TT-scheme h:Y→Th:Y\rightarrow T such that fT=p​rT:XT=X×S∗T→Tf_{T}=\mathrm{p}r_{T}:X_{T}=X\times_{S_{*}}T\rightarrow T factors as

fT=h∘ρ:XT⟶ρY⟶hTf_{T}=h\circ\rho:X_{T}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rho}}{{\longrightarrow}}Y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle h}}{{\longrightarrow}}T

where ρ:XT→Y\rho:X_{T}\rightarrow Y is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration.

Proof.

Shrinking SS if necessary, we may assume that SS is affine, that f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S is smooth and that κ⁡(Xs)<0\kappa(X_{s})<0 for every closed point s∈Ss\in S. Letting TT be the normalization of SS in LL and shrinking TT again if necessary, we obtain a finite étale morphism T→ST\rightarrow S such that the generic fiber of prT:XT→T\mathrm{pr}_{T}:X_{T}\rightarrow T is isomorphic to the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibered surface ρ:Xη×Spec⁡(K)Spec⁡(L)→C\rho:X_{\eta}\times_{\mathrm{Spec}(K)}\mathrm{Spec}(L)\rightarrow C and then the assertion follows from Lemma 7 below.

Since XX and SS are affine and of finite type over kk, there exists a subfield k0k_{0} of kk of finite transcendence degree over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, and a smooth morphism f0:X0→S0f_{0}:X_{0}\rightarrow S_{0} of k0k_{0}-varieties such that f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S is obtained from f0:X0→S0f_{0}:X_{0}\rightarrow S_{0} by the base extension Spec⁡(k)→Spec⁡(k0)\mathrm{Spec}\left(k\right)\rightarrow\mathrm{Spec}(k_{0}). In the proof of the above theorem, we used the following lemma:

Lemma 7.

Let f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S be a dominant affine morphism between normal varieties defined over a field kk of characteristic zero. Then the following are equivalent:

in which each square is cartesian. 2.2. Deformations of irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces


In this subsection, we consider the particular situation of a flat family f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S over a normal variety SS whose general fibers are irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces. A combination of Corollary 5 and Theorem 6 above implies that if f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S is smooth and defined over a field of infinite transcendence degree over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, then the generic fiber XηX_{\eta} of ff is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled. Equivalently, there exists an open subset S∗⊂SS_{*}\subset S and a normal S∗S_{*}-scheme h:Y→S∗h:Y\rightarrow S_{*} such that the restriction of ff to X∗=X×SS∗X_{*}=X\times_{S}S_{*} factors through an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X∗→Y\rho:X_{*}\rightarrow Y (see Lemma 7). The restriction of ρ\rho to the fiber of ff over a general closed point s∈S0s\in S_{0} is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρs:Xs→Ys\rho_{s}:X_{s}\rightarrow Y_{s} over the normal, whence smooth, curve YsY_{s}. Since XsX_{s} is irrational, YsY_{s} is irrational, and so ρs:Xs→Ys\rho_{s}:X_{s}\rightarrow Y_{s} is the unique 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration on XsX_{s} up to composition by automorphisms of YsY_{s}. So in this case, we can identify ρs:Xs→Ys\rho_{s}:X_{s}\rightarrow Y_{s} with the Maximally Rationally Connected fibration (MRC-fibration) φ:X¯s⇢Ys\varphi:\overline{X}_{s}\dashrightarrow Y_{s} of a smooth projective model X¯s\overline{X}_{s} of XsX_{s} in the sense of [11, IV.5]: recall that φ\varphi is unique, characterized by the property that its general fibers are rationally connected and that for a very general point y∈Ysy\in Y_{s} any rational curve in X¯s\overline{X}_{s} which meets X¯y\overline{X}_{y} is actually contained in X¯y\overline{X}_{y}. The 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X∗→Y\rho:X_{*}\rightarrow Y can therefore be re-interpreted as being the MRC-fibration of a relative smooth projective model X¯\overline{X} of XX over SS.

Reversing the argument, general existence and uniqueness results for MRC-fibrations allow actually to get rid of the smoothness hypothesis of a general fiber of f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S and to extend the conclusion of Theorem 6 to arbitrary base fields of characteristic zero. Namely, we obtain the following characterization:

Theorem 9.

Let XX and SS be normal varieties defined over a field kk of characteristic zero and let f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S be a dominant affine morphism with the property that for a general closed point s∈Ss\in S, the fiber XsX_{s} is irrational and 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled. Then there exists an open subset S∗S_{*} and a normal S∗S_{*}-scheme h:Y→S∗h:Y\rightarrow S_{*} such that the restriction of ff to X∗=X×SS∗X_{*}=X\times_{S}S_{*} factors as

f∣X∗=h∘ρ:X∗⟶ρY⟶hS∗f\mid_{X_{*}}=h\circ\rho:X_{*}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rho}}{{\longrightarrow}}Y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle h}}{{\longrightarrow}}S_{*}

where ρ:X∗→Y\rho:X_{*}\rightarrow Y is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration.

Proof.

Shrinking SS if necessary, we may assume that for every closed point s∈Ss\in S, XsX_{s} is irrational and 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled, hence carrying a unique 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πs:Xs→Cs\pi_{s}:X_{s}\rightarrow C_{s} over an irrational normal curve CsC_{s}. Since f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S is affine, there exists a normal projective SS-scheme X¯→S\overline{X}\rightarrow S and an open embedding X↪X¯X\hookrightarrow\overline{X} of schemes over SS. Letting W→X¯W\rightarrow\overline{X} be a resolution of the singularities of X¯\overline{X}, we may assume up to shrinking SS again if necessary that W→SW\rightarrow S is a smooth morphism. We let j:X⇢Wj:X\dashrightarrow W be the birational map of SS-schemes induced by the embedding X↪X¯X\hookrightarrow\overline{X}. By virtue of [11, Theorem 5.9], there exists an open subset W′W^{\prime} of WW, an SS-scheme h:Z→Sh:Z\rightarrow S and a proper morphism q¯:W′→Z\overline{q}:W^{\prime}\rightarrow Z such that for every s∈Ss\in S, the induced rational map q¯s:Ws⇢Zs\overline{q}_{s}:W_{s}\dashrightarrow Z_{s} is the MRC-fibration for WsW_{s}. On the other hand, since WsW_{s} is a smooth projective model of XsX_{s}, the induced rational map πs:X¯s⇢Cs\pi_{s}:\overline{X}_{s}\dashrightarrow C_{s} is the MRC-fibration for WsW_{s}. Consequently, for a general closed point z∈Zz\in Z with h⁡(z)=sh(z)=s, the fiber WzW_{z} of q¯s\overline{q}_{s}, which is an irreducible proper rational curve contained in WsW_{s}, must coincide with the closure of the image by jj of a general closed fiber of πs\pi_{s}. The latter being isomorphic to the affine line 𝔸κ1\mathbb{A}_{\kappa}^{1} over the residue field κ\kappa of the corresponding point of CsC_{s}, we conclude that there exists an affine open subset UU of XX on which the composition q¯∘j:U→Z\overline{q}\circ j:U\rightarrow Z is a well defined morphism with general closed fibers isomorphic to affine lines over the corresponding residue fields. So q¯∘j:U→Z\overline{q}\circ j:U\rightarrow Z is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration bu virtue of [9]. The generic fiber of f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S is thus 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled and the assertion follows from Lemma 7 above. ∎

Letting X=X¯∖DX=\overline{X}\setminus D, we obtain a smooth family

f=g∘ρ¯∣X:X⟶ρ¯∣XY→hSf=g\circ\overline{\rho}\mid_{X}:X\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\overline{\rho}\mid_{X}}}{{\longrightarrow}}Y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle h}}{{\rightarrow}}S

where ρ¯∣X:X→Y\overline{\rho}\mid_{X}:X\rightarrow Y is nontrivial, locally trivial, 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle such that for every s∈Ss\in S, XsX_{s} is an affine surface with an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρs:Xs→Ys\rho_{s}:X_{s}\rightarrow Y_{s} of complete type.

In contrast with the previous example, the following proposition shows in particular that if the total space of a family of irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine surfaces f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S has finite divisor class group, then the induced 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration on a general fiber of f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S is of affine type.

Proposition 11.

Let XX be a geometrically integral normal variety with finite divisor class group Cl⁡(X)\mathrm{Cl}(X) and let f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S be a dominant affine morphism to a normal variety SS with the property that for a general closed point s∈Ss\in S, the fiber XsX_{s} is irrational and 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled, say with unique 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πs:Xs→Cs\pi_{s}:X_{s}\rightarrow C_{s}. Then there exists an effective 𝔾a,S\mathbb{G}_{a,S}-action on XX such that for a general closed point s∈Ss\in S, the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πs:Xs→Cs\pi_{s}:X_{s}\rightarrow C_{s} factors through the algebraic quotient ρs:Xs→Xs//𝔾a,s=Spec(Γ(Xs,𝒪Xs)𝔾a,s)\rho_{s}:X_{s}\rightarrow X_{s}/\!/\mathbb{G}_{a,s}=\mathrm{Spec}(\Gamma(X_{s},\mathcal{O}_{X_{s}})^{\mathbb{G}_{a,s}}).

Since ρ−1​(U)\rho^{-1}(U) is affine, its complement in XX is of pure codimension 11, and the finiteness of Cl⁡(X)\mathrm{Cl}(X) implies that it is actually the support of an effective principal divisor divX​(a)\mathrm{div}_{X}(a) for some a∈Γ⁡(X,𝒪X)a\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}). Letting ∂0\partial_{0} be the locally nilpotent derivation of Γ⁡(ρ−1​(U),𝒪X)≃Γ​(X,𝒪X)a\Gamma(\rho^{-1}(U),\mathcal{O}_{X})\simeq\Gamma(X,\mathcal{O}_{X})_{a} corresponding to the 𝔾a,U\mathbb{G}_{a,U}-action by translations on the second factor, the finite generation of Γ⁡(X,𝒪X)\Gamma(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}) guarantees that for a suitably chosen n≥0n\geq 0, an∂0a^{n}\partial_{0} lifts to a locally nilpotent derivation ∂\partial of Γ⁡(X,𝒪X)\Gamma(X,\mathcal{O}_{X}). By construction, the restriction of ff to the dense open subset ρ−1​(U)\rho^{-1}(U) of XX is invariant under the corresponding 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action, and so f:X→Sf:X\rightarrow S is 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-invariant. For a general closed point s∈Ss\in S, the induced 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on XsX_{s} is nontrivial, and its algebraic quotient ρs:Xs→Xs//𝔾a=Spec(Γ(Xs,𝒪Xs)𝔾a)\rho_{s}:X_{s}\rightarrow X_{s}/\!/\mathbb{G}_{a}=\mathrm{Spec}(\Gamma(X_{s},\mathcal{O}_{X_{s}})^{\mathbb{G}_{a}}) is a surjective 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration over a normal affine curve Xs//𝔾aX_{s}/\!/\mathbb{G}_{a}. 3. Affine threefolds fibered in irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled surfaces

In this section we consider in more detail the case of normal complex affine threefolds XX admitting a fibration f:X→Bf:X\rightarrow B by irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled surfaces, over a smooth curve BB. We explain how to derive the variety h:Y→Bh:Y\rightarrow B for which ff factors through an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X→Y\rho:X\rightarrow Y from a relative minimal model program applied to a suitable projective model of XX over BB. In the case where the divisor class group of XX is finite, we provide a complete classification of such fibrations in terms of additive group actions on XX.

3.1. 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-cylinders via relative Minimal Model Program


Let XX be a normal complex affine threefold and let f:X→Bf:X\rightarrow B be a flat morphism onto a smooth curve BB with the property that a general closed fiber XbX_{b} of ff is an irreducible irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled surface. We let f¯:W→B\overline{f}:W\rightarrow B be a smooth projective model of XX over BB obtained from an arbitrary normal relative projective completion X↪X¯X\hookrightarrow\overline{X} of XX over BB by resolving the singularities. We let j:X⇢Wj:X\dashrightarrow W be the birational map induced by the open immersion X↪X¯X\hookrightarrow\overline{X}.

By applying a minimal model program for WW over BB, we obtain a sequence of birational BB-maps

W=W0⇢φ1W1⇢φ2W2⇢⋯⇢Wℓ−1⇢φℓWℓ=W′,W=W_{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\varphi_{1}}}{{\dashrightarrow}}W_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\varphi_{2}}}{{\dashrightarrow}}W_{2}\dashrightarrow\cdots\dashrightarrow W_{\ell-1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\varphi_{\ell}}}{{\dashrightarrow}}W_{\ell}=W^{\prime},

between BB-schemes f¯i:Wi→B\overline{f}_{i}:W_{i}\rightarrow B, where φi:Wi⇢Wi+1\varphi_{i}:W_{i}\dashrightarrow W_{i+1} is either a divisorial contraction or a flip, and the rightmost variety W′W^{\prime} is the output of a minimal model program over BB. The hypotheses imply that W′W^{\prime} has the structure of a Mori conic bundle ρ¯:W′→Y\overline{\rho}:W^{\prime}\rightarrow Y over a BB-scheme h:Y→Bh:Y\rightarrow B corresponding to the contraction of an extremal ray of NE¯​(W′/B)\overline{\mathrm{NE}}(W^{\prime}/B). Indeed, a general fiber of f¯\overline{f} being a birationaly ruled projective surface, the output W′W^{\prime} is not a minimal model of WW over BB. So W′W^{\prime} is either a Moric conic bundle over a BB-scheme YY of dimension 22 or a del Pezzo fibration over BB, the second case being excluded by the fact that the general fibers of f¯\overline{f} are irrational.

Proposition 12.

The induced map ρ=ρ¯∣X:X⇢Y\rho=\overline{\rho}\mid_{X}:X\dashrightarrow Y is a rational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration.

Proof.

Since a general closed fiber XbX_{b} is a normal affine surface with an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πb:Xb→Cb\pi_{b}:X_{b}\rightarrow C_{b} over a certain irrational smooth curve CbC_{b}, it follows that there exists a unique maximal affine open subset UbU_{b} of CbC_{b} such that πb−1​(Ub)≃Ub×𝔸1\pi_{b}^{-1}(U_{b})\simeq U_{b}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} and such that the rational map jb:πb−1​(Ub)⇢Wbj_{b}:\pi_{b}^{-1}(U_{b})\dashrightarrow W_{b} induced by jj is regular, inducing an isomorphism between πb−1​(Ub)\pi_{b}^{-1}(U_{b}) and its image. Each step φi:Wi⇢Wi+1\varphi_{i}:W_{i}\dashrightarrow W_{i+1} consists of either a flip whose flipping and flipped curves are contained in fibers of f¯i:Wi→B\overline{f}_{i}:W_{i}\rightarrow B and f¯i+1:Wi+1→B\overline{f}_{i+1}:W_{i+1}\rightarrow B respectively, or a divisorial contraction whose exceptional divisor is contained in a fiber of f¯i:Wi→B\overline{f}_{i}:W_{i}\rightarrow B, or a divisorial contraction whose exceptional divisor intersects a general fiber of f¯i:Wi→B\overline{f}_{i}:W_{i}\rightarrow B. Clearly, a general closed fiber of f¯i:Wi→B\overline{f}_{i}:W_{i}\rightarrow B is not affected by the first two types of birational maps. On the other hand, if φi:Wi→Wi+1\varphi_{i}:W_{i}\rightarrow W_{i+1} is the contraction of a divisor Ei⊂WiE_{i}\subset W_{i} which dominates BB, then a general fiber of φi∣Ei\varphi_{i}\mid_{E_{i}} is a smooth proper rational curve. The intersection of EiE_{i} with a general closed fiber Wi,bW_{i,b} of f¯i\overline{f}_{i} thus consists of proper rational curves, and its intersection with the image of the maximal affine cylinder like open subset πb−1​(Ub)\pi_{b}^{-1}(U_{b}) of XbX_{b} is either empty or composed of affine rational curves. Since UbU_{b} is an irrational curve, it follows that each irreducible component of Ei∩(πb−1​(Ub))E_{i}\cap(\pi_{b}^{-1}(U_{b})) is contained in a fiber of πb\pi_{b}. This implies that there exists an open subset Ub,0U_{b,0} of UbU_{b} with the property that for every i=1,…,ℓi=1,\ldots,\ell, the restriction of φi∘⋯∘φ1∘j\varphi_{i}\circ\cdots\circ\varphi_{1}\circ j to πb−1​(Ub,0)⊂Xb\pi_{b}^{-1}(U_{b,0})\subset X_{b} is an isomorphism onto its image in Wi,bW_{i,b}. A general fiber of ρ¯:W′→Y\overline{\rho}:W^{\prime}\rightarrow Y over a closed point y∈Yy\in Y being a smooth proper rational curve, its intersection with πh⁡(y)−1​(Uh⁡(y),0)\pi_{h(y)}^{-1}(U_{h(y),0}) viewed as an open subset of Wh⁡(y)′W^{\prime}_{h(y)}, is thus either empty or equal to a fiber of πh⁡(y)\pi_{h(y)}. So by virtue of [9], there exists an open subset VV of XX on which ρ¯\overline{\rho} restricts to an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ¯∣V:V→Y\overline{\rho}\mid_{V}:V\rightarrow Y. ∎

Corollary 13.

Let XX be a normal complex affine threefold XX equipped with a morphism f:X→Bf:X\rightarrow B onto a smooth curve BB whose general closed fibers are irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled surfaces. Then XX is birationaly equivalent to the product of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} with a family h0:𝒞0→B0h_{0}:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow B_{0} of smooth projective curves of genus g≥1g\geq 1 over an open subset B0⊂BB_{0}\subset B.

Proof.

By the previous Proposition, XX has the structure of a rational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration ρ:X⇢Y\rho:X\dashrightarrow Y over a 22-dimensional normal proper BB-scheme h:Y→Bh:Y\rightarrow B. In particular, XX is birational to Y×ℙ1Y\times\mathbb{P}^{1}. On the other hand, for a general closed point b∈Bb\in B, the curve YbY_{b} is birational to the base CbC_{b} of the unique 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πb:Xb→Cb\pi_{b}:X_{b}\rightarrow C_{b} on the irrational affine surface XbX_{b}. Letting σ:Y~→Y\sigma:\tilde{Y}\rightarrow Y be a desingularization of YY, there exists an open subset B0B_{0} of BB over which the composition h∘σ:Y~→Yh\circ\sigma:\tilde{Y}\rightarrow Y restricts to a smooth family h0:𝒞0→B0h_{0}:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow B_{0} of projective curves of a certain genus g≥1g\geq 1. By construction, XX is birational to 𝒞0×ℙ1\mathcal{C}_{0}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}. ∎

Remark 14.

Example 10 above shows conversely that for every smooth family h:𝒞→Bh:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow B of projective curves of genus g≥2g\geq 2, there exists a smooth 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled affine threefold XX birationaly equivalent to 𝒞×ℙ1\mathcal{C}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}. Actually, in the setting of the previous Corollary 13, if we assume further that a general fiber of f:X→Bf:X\rightarrow B carries an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πb:Xb→Cb\pi_{b}:X_{b}\rightarrow C_{b} over a smooth curve CbC_{b} whose smooth projective model has genus g≥2g\geq 2, then there exists a uniquely determined family h:𝒞→Bh:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow B of proper stable curves of genus gg such that XX is birationaly equivalent to 𝒞×ℙ1\mathcal{C}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}: indeed, the moduli stack ℳ¯g\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{g} of stable curves of genus g≥2g\geq 2 being proper and separated, the smooth family h0:𝒞0→B0h_{0}:\mathcal{C}_{0}\rightarrow B_{0} extends in a unique way to a family h:𝒞→Bh:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow B of stable curves of genus gg.

3.2. Factorial threefolds

Proposition 15.

Let XX be a normal affine threefold with finite divisor class group Cl⁡(X)\mathrm{Cl}(X) and let f:X→Bf:X\rightarrow B be a morphism onto a smooth curve BB whose general closed fibers are irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled surfaces. Then there exists a factorisation f=h∘ρ:X→Y→Bf=h\circ\rho:X\rightarrow Y\rightarrow B where ρ:X→Y\rho:X\rightarrow Y is the algebraic quotient morphism of an effective 𝔾a,B\mathbb{G}_{a,B}-action on XX. In particular, a general fiber of ff admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration of affine type.

Proof.

By virtue of Proposition 11, there exist an effective 𝔾a,B\mathbb{G}_{a,B}-action on XX such that for a general closed point b∈Bb\in B, the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πb:Xb→Cb\pi_{b}:X_{b}\rightarrow C_{b} on XbX_{b} factors through the algebraic quotient ρb:Xb→Xb//𝔾a,b=Spec(Γ(Xb,𝒪Xb)𝔾a,b)\rho_{b}:X_{b}\rightarrow X_{b}/\!/\mathbb{G}_{a,b}=\mathrm{Spec}(\Gamma(X_{b},\mathcal{O}_{X_{b}})^{\mathbb{G}_{a,b}}). Since XX is a threefold, the ring of invariants Γ​(X,𝒪X)𝔾a,B\Gamma(X,\mathcal{O}_{X})^{\mathbb{G}_{a,B}} is finitely generated [16]. The quotient morphism ρ:X→Y=Spec⁡(Γ​(X,𝒪X)𝔾a,B)\rho:X\rightarrow Y=\mathrm{Spec}(\Gamma(X,\mathcal{O}_{X})^{\mathbb{G}_{a,B}}) is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration, and since YY is a categorical quotient in the category of algebraic varieties, the invariant morphism f:X→Bf:X\rightarrow B factors through ρ\rho. ∎

Corollary 16.

Let f:𝔸3→Bf:\mathbb{A}^{3}\rightarrow B be a morphism onto a smooth curve BB with irrational 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-ruled general fibers. Then BB is isomorphic to either ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} or 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} and there exists a factorization f=h∘ρ:𝔸3→𝔸2→Bf=h\circ\rho:\mathbb{A}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{2}\rightarrow B, where ρ:𝔸3→𝔸2\rho:\mathbb{A}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{2} is the quotient morphism of an effective 𝔾a,B\mathbb{G}_{a,B}-action on 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3}.

Proof.

Since BB is dominated by a general line in 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3}, it is necessarily isomorphic to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} or 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}. The second assertion follows from Proposition 15 and the fact that the algebraic quotient of every nontrivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} is isomorphic to 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} [13]. ∎

Example 17.

In Corollary 16 above, the base curve BB need not be affine. For instance, the morphism

f:𝔸3=Spec(ℂ[x,y,z])⟶ℙ1,(x,y,z)↦[((xz−y2)x2+1:(xz−y2)3]f:\mathbb{A}^{3}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z])\longrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1},(x,y,z)\mapsto[((xz-y^{2})x^{2}+1:(xz-y^{2})^{3}]

defines a family whose general member is isomorphic to the product Cλ×𝔸1C_{\lambda}\times\mathbb{A}^{1} where Cλ⊂𝔸2=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x​z−y2,x])C_{\lambda}\subset\mathbb{A}^{2}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[xz-y^{2},x]) is the affine elliptic curve with equation (x​z−y2)3+λ⁡((x​z−y2)​x2+1)=0(xz-y^{2})^{3}+\lambda((xz-y^{2})x^{2}+1)=0. The subring ℂ⁡[x​z−y2,x]\mathbb{C}[xz-y^{2},x] of ℂ⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] coincides with the ring of invariants of the 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action associated with the locally nilpotent ℂ⁡[x]\mathbb{C}[x]-derivation x∂y+2y∂zx\partial_{y}+2y\partial_{z} and ff is the composition of the quotient morphism ρ:𝔸3→𝔸2=𝔸3//𝔾a=Spec(ℂ[u,v])\rho:\mathbb{A}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{2}=\mathbb{A}^{3}/\!/\mathbb{G}_{a}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[u,v]), (x,y,z)↦(x​z−y2,x)(x,y,z)\mapsto(xz-y^{2},x) and the morphism h:𝔸2=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[u,v])→ℙ1h:\mathbb{A}^{2}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[u,v])\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1}, (u,v)↦[uv2+1:u3]\left(u,v\right)\mapsto[uv^{2}+1:u^{3}].

Corollary 16 above implies in particular that a general fiber of a regular function f:𝔸3→𝔸1f:\mathbb{A}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1} cannot be an irrational surface equipped with an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration of complete type only. In contrast, regular functions f:𝔸3→𝔸1f:\mathbb{A}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1} whose general fibers are rational and equipped with 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations of complete type only do exist, as illustrated by the following example.

Example 18.

Let f=x3−y3+z⁡(z+1)∈ℂ⁡[x,y,z]f=x^{3}-y^{3}+z(z+1)\in\mathbb{C}[x,y,z] and let f:𝔸3=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[x,y,z])→𝔸1=Spec⁡(ℂ⁡[λ])f:\mathbb{A}^{3}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z])\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}=\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[\lambda]) be the corresponding morphism. The closure S¯λ\overline{S}_{\lambda} in ℙ3=Proj⁡(ℂ⁡[x,y,z,t])\mathbb{P}^{3}=\mathrm{Proj}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,t]) of a general fiber Sλ=f∗​(λ)S_{\lambda}=f^{*}(\lambda) of ff is a smooth cubic surface which intersects the hyperplane H∞={t=0}H_{\infty}=\left\{t=0\right\} along the union BλB_{\lambda} of three lines meeting at the Eckardt point p=[0:0:1:0]p=\left[0:0:1:0\right]. Thus SλS_{\lambda} is rational and a direct computation reveals that κ⁡(Sλ)=−∞\kappa(S_{\lambda})=-\infty. So by virtue [14], SλS_{\lambda} admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πλ:Sλ→Cλ\pi_{\lambda}:S_{\lambda}\rightarrow C_{\lambda} over a smooth rational curve CλC_{\lambda}. If CλC_{\lambda} was affine, then there would exist a non trivial 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on SλS_{\lambda} having the general fibers of πλ\pi_{\lambda} as general orbits. But it is straightforward to check that every automorphism of SλS_{\lambda} considered as a birational self-map of S¯λ\overline{S}_{\lambda} is in fact a biregular automorphism of S¯λ\overline{S}_{\lambda} preserving the boundary BλB_{\lambda}. So the automorphism group of SλS_{\lambda} injects into the group Aut⁡(S¯λ,Bλ)\mathrm{Aut}(\overline{S}_{\lambda},B_{\lambda}) of automorphisms of the pair (S¯λ,Bλ)(\overline{S}_{\lambda},B_{\lambda}). The latter being a finite group, we conclude that no such 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action exists, and hence that SλS_{\lambda} only admits 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations of complete type. An 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πλ:Sλ→ℙ1\pi_{\lambda}:S_{\lambda}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} can be obtained as follows: letting Bλ=L1∪L2∪L3B_{\lambda}=L_{1}\cup L_{2}\cup L_{3}, L1L_{1} is a member of a 66-tuple of pairwise disjoint lines whose simultaneous contraction realizes S¯λ\overline{S}_{\lambda} as a blow-up σ:S¯λ→ℙ2\sigma:\overline{S}_{\lambda}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{2} of ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} in such a way that σ⁡(L2)\sigma(L_{2}) and σ⁡(L3)\sigma(L_{3}) are respectively a smooth conic and its tangent line at the point p=σ⁡(L1)p=\sigma(L_{1}). The birational transform π¯λ:S¯λ⇢ℙ1\overline{\pi}_{\lambda}:\overline{S}_{\lambda}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} on S¯λ\overline{S}_{\lambda} of the pencil generated by σ⁡(L2)\sigma(L_{2}) and 2​σ​(L3)2\sigma(L_{3}) restricts to an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration πλ:Sλ→ℙ1\pi_{\lambda}:S_{\lambda}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} with two degenerate fibers: an irreducible one, of multiplicity two, consisting of the intersection with SλS_{\lambda} of the unique exceptional divisor of σ\sigma whose center is supported on σ⁡(L3)∖{p}\sigma(L_{3})\setminus\{p\}, and a smooth one consisting of the intersection with SλS_{\lambda} of the four exceptional divisors of σ\sigma with centers supported on σ⁡(L2)∖{p}\sigma(L_{2})\setminus\left\{p\right\}.
